t: Find Minimum Cost to Remove Array Elements
o: Repeatedly remove two of the first three elements paying the max of the two; when fewer than three remain, remove them all paying the max. Only the frontier matters: once elements before index i are gone, the future depends solely on nums[i..], so define dp[i] = min cost to clear the suffix starting at i. From state i with at least 3 elements left there are exactly three pair choices, each leaving the third element as the new head. Example 1: removing (6,8) costs 8 leaving [2,4], then 4, total 12.
k: State = starting index of the remaining suffix; only three transitions per state (which pair of the first three to remove).
Base case: suffix of length 1 or 2 costs its max element.
O(n) states, O(1) transitions — trivially fits n <= 1000.

a.i: dp[i] = min over the three pairs (i,i+1), (i,i+2), (i+1,i+2) of max(pair) + dp[i+2], with dp[n-1] = nums[n-1], dp[n-2] = max of last two. Iterate i downward.
s: For i from n-3 down to 0, dp[i] = min of three expressions max(nums[i],nums[i+1])+dp[i+2], max(nums[i],nums[i+2])+dp[i+2], max(nums[i+1],nums[i+2])+dp[i+2].
a.t: O(n) — one pass with constant work per index
a.sp: O(n) for the dp array (reducible to O(1) with two rolling variables)

w: Note that removing any pair from the first three always advances the frontier by exactly 2 (one element survives), which is why dp[i+2] appears in all transitions. Edge cases: n = 1 and n = 2 fall straight into the final-operation rule. Follow-up: reconstruct the actual sequence of removals by storing parent choices.
